analysis.investment_thesis: Cemindia Projects (formerly ITD Cementation) has delivered exceptional revenue growth — from INR 3,809 Cr (FY22) to INR 9,097 Cr (FY25), a ~33% CAGR — riding India's infrastructure super-cycle with specialized expertise in maritime, tunneling, and transit projects that few competitors can match. However, thin 7.74% operating margins, working-capital-intensive cash flows (FCF of just INR 30 Cr in FY25 despite INR 373 Cr profit), and EPC project risk temper my conviction.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of ~33% (FY22–FY25) and net profit growing from INR 69 Cr to INR 373 Cr in three years — genuinely exceptional growth
ROE of 21.8% and ROCE of 27.6% exceed my 20% threshold, reflecting improving capital efficiency as scale rises
Specialized niche in maritime infrastructure, TBM tunneling, and MRTs creates genuine barriers — few Indian EPC players can execute jetties, dry docks, and metro underground works simultaneously
key_risks: EPC business depends on lumpy government project awards; revenue can stall sharply if order inflow slows or delays occur
Operating margin of 7.74% leaves minimal buffer — cost overruns on any large project directly compress already thin profits
FCF of INR 30 Cr in FY25 against INR 373 Cr net profit reveals extreme working capital drag from receivables and retention money locked in government contracts
red_flags: Ownership transferred to Renew Exim DMCC (August 2025) — management continuity and strategic direction under new parent are unproven and warrant scuttlebutt investigation
Finance costs of INR 229 Cr growing in line with revenue growth, indicating leverage-driven rather than organically funded expansion
FCF compressed to near zero in FY25 despite highest-ever profits — a pattern common in aggressive EPC expansion that can stress balance sheets if projects slip
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Fisher standpoint, the growth profile is the most attractive among these five stocks: the company has found a niche in India's INR 100+ lakh crore infrastructure pipeline that requires genuine engineering depth. Maritime and underground work are not replicable quickly by commodity contractors, giving the firm pricing power and repeat government mandates. The recent management change under Renew Exim DMCC is the key unknown — I would spend considerable scuttlebutt effort speaking to project engineers, government procurement officers, and subcontractors before adding to any position.

The financial picture is mixed in a typical EPC way: high ROCE signals excellent project returns in theory, but the working capital trap (OCF INR 203 Cr vs. net profit INR 373 Cr in FY25) is real and growing. D/E at 0.48 is acceptable, but borrowings grew from INR 560 Cr (FY22) to INR 982 Cr (FY25). This is a business on the cusp of warranting a higher score if the new ownership proves capable and India's infrastructure spend remains robust — but I would wait for one more year of post-ownership results before upgrading.
